title: They Said No
narrativeQuestion: How did Chinese Americans resist exclusion?
answerPromise: Chinese Americans organized mass resistance and fought exclusion in court. Some of what they won now protects everyone in the United States.

chapters.title: How a City Forced People Out
chapters.claim: Tacoma turned exclusion into a public procedure run by elected officials, police, deadlines, and a forced march. Other communities copied it because it worked and nobody involved was punished.

namedPeople.name: Jacob Weisbach
namedPeople.anchorNote: No verified redistributable likeness derivative was acquired; the page uses attributed documents and events rather than an invented likeness.

chapters.title: The Government Cancels His Return
chapters.claim: The government issued Chae Chan Ping a return certificate, cancelled it while he was at sea, refused to honor it, and won unanimous approval from the Supreme Court.

namedPeople.name: Chae Chan Ping
namedPeople.anchorNote: No verified redistributable likeness derivative was acquired; the page uses attributed records rather than an invented likeness.

chapters.title: The Geary Act Demands Proof
chapters.claim: The registration law forced Chinese laborers to document their right to remain and imposed a racial witness condition in the court exception for missed registration.

namedPeople.name: Thomas J. Geary
namedPeople.anchorNote: Supporting lawmaker rather than the narrative subject of the scene.

chapters.title: Yick Wo Wins Equal Protection
chapters.claim: Lee Yick proved that a law fair on its face can still violate equal protection when officials enforce it with an unequal hand.

namedPeople.name: Lee Yick
namedPeople.anchorNote: No verified redistributable likeness derivative was acquired; the page uses the original court holding rather than an invented likeness.

chapters.title: One Hundred Thousand Refuse
chapters.claim: Chinese community organizations coordinated one of the largest acts of civil disobedience in nineteenth-century America, funding lawyers and urging laborers not to register.

chapters.title: Wong Kim Ark Wins Citizenship
chapters.claim: Wong Kim Ark won citizenship at birth under the Fourteenth Amendment for U.S.-born children of resident immigrant parents.

namedPeople.name: Wong Kim Ark
namedPeople.anchorNote: The original 1894 departure statement includes his photograph.

chapters.title: Exclusion Lasts Sixty-One Years
chapters.claim: Exclusion persisted for 61 elapsed years before repeal made Chinese immigrants eligible for naturalization and introduced an annual quota of 105.

accuracyNotes: The Geary certificate requirement covered laborers; the white-witness condition shown is the missed-registration court exception. Photographs were added in 1893.
Wong Kim Ark is taught as the 1898 holding for a U.S.-born child of resident immigrant parents, not as an unqualified statement about every present-day legal situation.
Plenary power does not mean that all judicial review is impossible.
Angel Island uses the foundation’s revised estimate of 100,000 Chinese detainees and a documented 756-day detention.
1882 through 1943 produces 62 annual labels across 61 elapsed years.
